[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal cohort study with existing genotype and dietary data (e.g., UK Biobank, NHANES) analyzing gene × diet interactions on weight loss maintenance in high-HOMA-IR individuals — Leverages large-scale observational data to assess whether the proposed three-way interaction (genotype, dietary glycemic load, insulin resistance) predicts sustained weight loss.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of PPARG/FTO variants, intermittent fasting, and glycemic load interventions, focusing on insulin-resistant subgroups — Synthesizes existing evidence to identify effect sizes, heterogeneity, and gaps, providing a theoretical foundation for the conditional hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Prospective cohort study of individuals with high baseline insulin resistance (HOMA-IR > 2.5) undergoing a controlled intermittent fasting protocol, with genotyping for PPARG and FTO variants — Provides primary evidence by measuring differential weight loss and insulin sensitivity changes over 6–12 months, controlling for adherence and dietary composition, to isolate genetic modulation of fasting efficacy.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacogenetic and nutrigenetic studies on PPARG and FTO interactions with dietary interventions (e.g., low-carbohydrate diets, time-restricted feeding) in insulin-resistant populations — Synthesizes existing but fragmented evidence on how these variants modify responses to dietary timing and macronutrient composition, identifying gaps and supporting or refuting the hypothesized inhibitory effect on intermittent fasting.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and cohort studies linking CLOCK gene polymorphisms (e.g., rs1801260, rs4580704) with metabolic outcomes (weight change, insulin sensitivity) in dietary interventions, particularly time-restricted feeding or intermittent fasting — Leverages large-scale published data to evaluate whether a consistent signal exists for CLOCK variants modifying fasting efficacy, providing statistical power to confirm or refute the hypothesis without new data collection.
